title: Zugzwang
subtitle: The obligation to move, turned into a weapon.
goals: Hand the move to your opponent
Win positions where every enemy move loses

steps.say: In most of chess, having the move is an advantage. In the endgame it is often a curse. This position is the TRÉBUCHET — the purest mutual zugzwang on the board. Neither king can approach the pawn, neither can improve. Whoever must move, loses. Study it for ten seconds: it is the atom from which most pawn endings are built.
Watch what happens when White is forced to move.

autoMoves.say: The king must step back — every square he has abandons the pawn...
...and Black escorts it home. White to move loses this position; Black to move loses it too. That is mutual zugzwang.

steps.prompt: Black was the one in zugzwang and had to step aside. Collect the reward!
hints: The pawn's only defender just walked away.

line.say: The pawn falls. Identical position to the diagram before, opposite result — the only difference was whose turn it was. In pawn endings, the move itself is a piece.

rejections.say: You stepped past the pawn and left it alive — ...Kc6 defends again and the trébuchet resets with YOU on move next time. When zugzwang hands you material, take it immediately.

steps.wrongSay: Black's king abandoned the pawn. Capture it.
steps.successSay: The trébuchet: whoever moves, loses. Now you know which side of it to be on.

steps.prompt: Zugzwang wins games outright, not just pawns. Mate in two — without giving check!
hints: Checking gives the king somewhere to go. Instead, cover his squares and force him to move himself into the net.
Qh4! Now Kf8 allows Qd8#, and any pawn move loses instantly too.

line.say: A pure waiting move. Black is not in check — he simply has no move that survives...
Checkmate delivered by the opponent's own obligation to move. When a king is boxed in, stop checking and start waiting.

rejections.say: Check — and the king gains freedom on h6 or f8. Every check against a boxed-in king is a favour to him. Take his squares away and hand him the move instead.

steps.wrongSay: Don't check. Find the quiet queen move that leaves Black no survivable reply.
steps.successSay: Zugzwang is the only tactic where your opponent does all the work.

steps.prompt: Blocked pawns, kings face to face. This is a draw — but only if you keep the opposition. Hold it!
hints: If you step aside, Black's king walks around your pawn and wins it. Stay in front and mirror him.
Kc3 keeps the king close to both key squares; the classic drawing method is to mirror Black's moves.

line.say: Correct — the king stays in touch with c4 and b3, mirroring Black. Neither side can make progress: every black attempt to outflank is met by a matching step. A draw held by understanding zugzwang rather than by luck.
The other mirror — the king shadows Black on the a-file side. As long as you match his king, the blocked pawns never fall.

rejections.say: One step too far back! Now ...Kc6-d5 outflanks you: the black king reaches c4 or a4 and wins the b4 pawn. In blocked pawn endings, distance from the key squares is everything.

steps.wrongSay: Stay close and mirror. Which king move keeps you touching the squares Black wants?
steps.successSay: Zugzwang cuts both ways — recognizing it saves as many games as it wins.
